newsitem.title: UK: EIB director sees London as top centre after EMU.
newsitem.headline: EIB director sees London as top centre after EMU.

text.p: The world's biggest borrower, the European Investment Bank, on Friday added its voice to those who say London will remain the top European financial centre after European economic and monetary union (EMU) is implemented.
EIB director general of finance Rene Karsenti told a conference in London this would hold whether or not Britain joined the single currency in 1999.
"Continental centres will benefit from EMU, especially due to the European Central Bank location (in Frankfurt), but it is likely London will keep most of its comparative advantages," Karsenti said.
"(London) has the world's largest forex market and has dominant shares in international equities, Eurobonds, swaps, banking and global asset management," he said.
"Its high concentration of bankers, lawyers, traders and accountants and its regulatory framework imply it will retain a comparative advantage over alternative centres on the continent," he said.

The EIB -- the financing arm of the European Union -- lends more than 20 billion Ecu per year to promote balanced development in Europe and borrows more than 18 billion Ecu annually in the capital markets.
Karsenti said Europe would see consolidation of bond and equity markets after EMU.

"Despite the continuous fall in information and transaction costs, which is making it feasible for trading to be more geographically dispersed, other factors, like the need for specialised personnel and computer services, suggest trading will continue to gravitate towards a single financial centre," he said.
Karsenti said if Britain did not join EMU London's position would not be greatly affected, at least not in the short term.
Further ahead, tax advantages elsewhere or limits to access by London-based banks to the proposed euro-payment system TARGET could have a negative impact on London's status, Karsenti said.
